topics.title: Trading Blocs and the World Trade Organisation
Market Failure in the Financial Sector
Macroeconomic Policies in a Global Context

cards.front: Define globalisation — and what characterises it?
cards.back:
Globalisation: the increasing integration and interdependence of the world's economies.

Its characteristics: increased free trade in goods and services across borders; increased foreign direct investment (FDI) and capital flows; increased foreign ownership of firms through multinational and transnational corporations; and increased freedom of movement of labour between countries.

cards.front: What factors have driven globalisation over the last 50 years?
cards.back:
• Trade liberalisation — falling tariffs and quotas (China's WTO entry in 2001 transformed its trade).
  • Advances in transport and communication technology.
  • The growth of MNCs building global supply chains (Apple, Amazon, Unilever).
  • Containerisation, which slashed shipping costs and time.
  • The deregulation of financial markets in the 1990s freeing capital flows.
  • Global institutions — the WTO, IMF and World Bank — promoting free trade and investment.

cards.front: Evaluate the impact of globalisation on consumers and workers.
cards.back:
Consumers gain lower prices, greater variety and better quality from competition — but face cultural imperialism, quality concerns over imports, and less choice long-term if domestic firms close.

Workers gain employment opportunities in developing countries and higher wages where skills are scarce — but lose jobs in developed countries as production relocates, and free movement of labour can mean lower wages and job insecurity for some.

cards.front: Evaluate the impact of globalisation on firms, governments and the environment.
cards.back:
• Domestic firms gain larger markets, imported inputs, skilled labour, economies of scale and foreign capital — but face fiercer competition, costlier skilled labour and fragile global supply chains.
  • Governments and the economy: growth, tax revenue and jobs on one side; income inequality, exposure to external shocks, and two-way pressure on the balance of payments and inflation on the other.
  • The environment loses: more production, transport, emissions and resource exploitation.

cards.front: Distinguish absolute advantage from comparative advantage.
cards.back:
Absolute advantage: a country can produce more of a good with the same resources than another country — a matter of productivity and efficiency.

Comparative advantage: a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country. The theory of comparative advantage says countries should specialise where their opportunity cost is lowest — raising the efficiency of resource allocation and total global output.

cards.front: Show comparative advantage using two countries' PPFs.
cards.back:
Germany's PPF runs from 150mn T-shirts to 20mn chips; Vietnam's from 200mn T-shirts to 10mn chips — each has an absolute advantage in one good.

Opportunity costs:

  • A chip costs Germany 7.5 T-shirts but Vietnam 20.
  • A T-shirt costs Vietnam 0.05 chips but Germany 0.13.

Each specialises where its opportunity cost is lower: fully specialised, they produce 20m chips and 200mn T-shirts — beating the 15m and 175mn made without specialisation — and by trading, both consume beyond their own PPFs.
cards.svgAlt: Two straight-line PPFs for computer chips and T-shirts crossing on shared axes: Germany's runs from 150 million T-shirts to 20 million chips, Vietnam's from 200 million T-shirts to 10 million chips

cards.front: Country A can make 40m cars or 80m tonnes of wheat; Country B can make 10m cars or 60m tonnes of wheat. Calculate each opportunity cost — who should specialise in what?
cards.back:
Opportunity cost of a car:

  • A gives up 80 ÷ 40 = 2 tonnes.
  • B gives up 60 ÷ 10 = 6 tonnes.

Opportunity cost of a tonne of wheat:

  • A gives up 0.5 cars.
  • B gives up 10 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.17 cars.

A has the lower opportunity cost in cars, B in wheat — so A specialises in cars and B in wheat, even though A has an absolute advantage in both.

cards.front: What are the assumptions of the comparative advantage model?
cards.back:
• Zero transport costs.
  • Perfect knowledge of prices, technology and resources.
  • Factor mobility within countries, so resources can switch industries freely.
  • Constant returns to scale, so doubling inputs doubles outputs.
  • No trade barriers — no tariffs or quotas.

Each assumption is a limitation: where transport is costly, factors are immobile or barriers exist, the predicted gains from specialisation shrink.

cards.front: Evaluate specialisation and trade in an international context.
cards.back:
For

  • Production at lower opportunity cost raises efficiency and global output.
  • Competition lowers prices.
  • Consumers get variety.
  • Access to bigger markets drives growth, innovation and investment.

Against

  • Dependency on imports for essentials leaves countries exposed to supply-chain shocks.
  • Uncompetitive domestic industries shed jobs.
  • Gains split unevenly between skilled and unskilled workers and between countries.
  • More production and transport damages the environment.
  • Lower labour standards abroad can mean worker exploitation.

cards.front: Define the pattern of trade.
cards.back:
The pattern of trade: the changing composition and direction of a country's exports and imports.

It answers two questions — what goods and services a country trades, and with which countries it trades them.

cards.front: What factors change the pattern of trade over time?
cards.back:
• Comparative advantage shifts — the UK's loss of it in manufacturing turned manufactured goods from exports into imports.
  • Emerging economies — the rise of China and India has claimed a growing share of world exports and imports.
  • Trade blocs and bilateral agreements redirect trade between members — the UK's exit from the EU cut EU trade and raised non-EU trade.
  • Relative exchange rates — a depreciation of the pound makes UK exports more competitive, raising exports and cutting imports.

cards.front: State the terms of trade formula — and what does a rise in the index mean?
cards.back:
The terms of trade (ToT) measures the relative price of a country's exports compared with its imports:

ToT index = (index of average export prices ÷ index of average import prices) × 100.

A rise means each unit of exports buys more imports — an improvement; a fall means it buys fewer — a deterioration.
cards.formulaHtml: Termsoftradeindex=(indexofaverageexportprices÷indexofaverageimportprices)×100Terms of trade index = (index of average export prices ÷ index of average import prices) × 100Termsoftradeindex=(indexofaverageexportprices÷indexofaverageimportprices)×100

cards.front: A country's export price index rises from 100 to 108 while its import price index rises from 100 to 120. Calculate the new terms of trade — improvement or deterioration?
cards.back:
ToT = (108 ÷ 120) × 100 = 90.

A fall from the base of 100 is a deterioration: export prices rose, but import prices rose faster, so each unit of exports now buys fewer imports. What moves the terms of trade is the ratio of the two indices — not the direction of either one alone.

cards.front: Evaluate the impact of a change in the terms of trade.
cards.back:
The effects hinge on the PED of exports.

An improvement lets each unit of exports buy more imports, potentially raising living standards — but if export demand is elastic, dearer exports lose so much volume that export revenue, the current account and GDP all suffer.

A deterioration cuts what exports can buy — but with elastic demand, cheaper exports can raise sales enough to lift export revenue, GDP and employment.

cards.front: Name the four types of trading bloc in rising order of integration.
cards.back:
• Free trade area (USMCA): members remove tariffs and quotas between themselves; each keeps its own trade policy with non-members.
  • Customs union (MERCOSUR): adds a common external tariff.
  • Common market (EU): adds free movement of factors of production — labour and capital.
  • Monetary union (Eurozone): adds a single currency.

Each step surrenders more national policy control.

cards.front: Distinguish trade creation from trade diversion — and what else do regional trade agreements bring?
cards.back:
Trade creation: trade shifts from a high-cost domestic producer to a lower-cost producer in another member country — efficiency and welfare rise.

Trade diversion: trade shifts from a lower-cost producer outside the bloc to a higher-cost producer within it — efficiency and welfare fall.

Other benefits: economies of scale, competition, consumer choice, political cooperation.

Other costs: loss of sovereignty, unequal gains between members, and dependency on the bloc.

cards.front: What conditions make a monetary union successful?
cards.back:
• Synchronised business cycles, so one interest rate suits all members when shocks hit.
  • Labour mobility, so workers can move to where the jobs are.
  • Fiscal transfers, so a central budget can support regions a shock hurts.
  • Mobility of capital and finance to follow investment opportunities across the union.

The Eurozone is the reference case — and its strains trace to these conditions holding only partially.

cards.front: What is the role of the WTO — and how can it conflict with trading blocs?
cards.back:
The World Trade Organisation promotes trade liberalisation and oversees global trade rules: a negotiating forum for reducing tariffs and quotas internationally, and a dispute settlement body that acts as a court between member countries.

The tension: regional blocs favour their members, which cuts against the WTO's broader aim of non-discrimination in global trade.

cards.front: Why do governments restrict free trade?
cards.back:
To protect:

  • Infant industries until they can compete.
  • Strategic industries vital to national security.
  • Sunset industries in decline, buying workers time to transition.
  • Jobs in high-employment sectors.

Also:

  • To prevent dumping — foreign producers selling below cost to grab market share.
  • To improve the balance of payments by cutting imports.
  • To enforce environmental and labour standards on what enters the country.

cards.front: Name the four methods of protectionism.
cards.back:
• Tariff: a tax on imports. It raises the price of imported goods, making domestic goods relatively cheaper.
  • Quota: a physical limit on how much of a good can be imported, restricting supply and raising the import price.
  • Subsidies to domestic producers: lower domestic production costs so home firms can compete with imports.
  • Non-tariff barriers: product standards, health and safety rules and administrative procedures that make importing harder and costlier.

cards.front: Show the impact of a tariff — prices, quantities and the three areas.
cards.back:
The tariff lifts the world supply price from P1 (Sworld) to P2 (Sworld+tariff): domestic output extends from Q1 to Q2, consumption contracts from Q4 to Q3, and imports shrink from Q4 − Q1 to Q3 − Q2.

The green area is the gain in domestic producer surplus, the purple rectangle is government tariff revenue, and the two red triangles are the net welfare loss — consumer surplus destroyed that nobody captures.
cards.svgAlt: Tariff diagram with domestic supply and demand and two horizontal world supply lines: the tariff raises the price from P1 to P2, with a green producer surplus gain, a purple tariff revenue rectangle and two red welfare loss triangles

cards.front: Evaluate protectionist policies.
cards.back:
Their effect depends on the elasticity of import demand — inelastic demand means tariffs barely cut imports — and on whether domestic producers can actually expand to replace them; if not, prices simply rise further.

Then the risks:

  • Retaliation from trading partners escalating into trade wars that hurt both sides.
  • The long-run cost — sheltering inefficient firms dulls the incentive to innovate and lift productivity.

cards.front: Define the balance of payments — and what does each account record?
cards.back:
Balance of payments (BoP): records all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world. Inflows are credits, outflows debits.

  • The current account: trade in goods and services, primary income (profits, interest, dividends) and secondary income (aid, remittances).
  • The capital account: minor capital transfers such as debt forgiveness.
  • The financial account: FDI, portfolio investment and changes in foreign exchange reserves.

cards.front: A country records: trade in goods — credits £260bn, debits £340bn; services — £310bn, £250bn; primary income — £75bn, £60bn; secondary income — £25bn, £45bn. Calculate the current account balance.
cards.back:
• Goods: 260 − 340 = −£80bn
  • Services: 310 − 250 = +£60bn
  • Primary income: 75 − 60 = +£15bn
  • Secondary income: 25 − 45 = −£20bn

Balance: −80 + 60 + 15 − 20 = −£25bn — a current account deficit.

The goods deficit is partly offset by surpluses on services and primary income: always net all four components.

cards.front: What causes a current account deficit — and how is one financed?
cards.back:
Causes:

  • Low competitiveness (dearer or poorer-quality domestic goods).
  • A strong exchange rate (cheap imports, dear exports).
  • High domestic demand sucking in imports.
  • Structural factors such as a long-term decline in manufacturing.

Since the balance of payments must always balance, a current account deficit (X < M) is financed by a surplus on the capital and financial accounts — and vice versa for a surplus.

cards.front: Evaluate the three policy routes for reducing a current account deficit.
cards.back:
• Expenditure-switching (tariffs, quotas, devaluation) redirects demand towards domestic output — effective short-term, but risks retaliation and higher consumer prices.
  • Expenditure-reducing (contractionary fiscal policy, higher interest rates) cuts overall demand and with it imports — at the cost of slower growth and higher unemployment.
  • Supply-side policies (education, R&D, infrastructure) rebuild export competitiveness — the durable fix, but slow and expensive.

cards.front: Why do persistent global imbalances matter?
cards.back:
Persistent deficits build up foreign debt — eventually demanding higher taxes or spending cuts — and can erode confidence in the currency, bringing depreciation and weaker FDI inflows.

Persistent surpluses feed inflationary pressure through high aggregate demand, and breed over-reliance on exports — leaving the economy exposed to global recessions and swings in trading partners' demand.

cards.front: Name the three exchange rate systems — and the vocabulary for a rise or fall in each.
cards.back:
• Floating: an exchange rate system determined by market forces of demand and supply for a currency, with no government intervention — the currency appreciates or depreciates.
  • Fixed: the central bank fixes the currency's value, often pegging it to another currency — the bank revalues or devalues.
  • Managed: fixed within a range, floating inside it.

Market-driven moves are appreciation/depreciation; deliberate central-bank moves are revaluation/devaluation.

cards.front: Show an appreciation of a floating currency — and what shifts the demand for it?
cards.back:
Higher demand for the currency shifts D1 right to D2 along the fixed supply curve: the exchange rate rises from P1 to P2 — an appreciation.

Demand rises with:

  • Higher relative interest rates (hot money inflows).
  • Lower relative inflation.
  • A current account surplus.
  • FDI inflows.
  • Speculation that the currency will strengthen.
cards.svgAlt: Currency market diagram with demand for the currency shifting right from D1 to D2 along a fixed supply curve, raising the exchange rate from P1 to P2

cards.front: Show a depreciation of a floating currency — and what shifts the supply of it?
cards.back:
Higher supply of the currency shifts S1 right to S2 along the fixed demand curve: the exchange rate falls from P1 to P2 — a depreciation.

Supply rises with quantitative easing (an expanded money supply) and with sales of the currency — including speculative selling when investors expect it to weaken; changes in foreign currency reserves also move the rate.
cards.svgAlt: Currency market diagram with the supply of the currency shifting right from S1 to S2 along a fixed demand curve, lowering the exchange rate from P1 to P2

cards.front: How do central banks intervene in currency markets?
cards.back:
Buying or selling the currency: buying its own currency raises demand and causes a revaluation; selling increases supply and causes a devaluation.

Interest rates: raising them attracts hot money inflows and revalues the currency; cutting them triggers outflows and devalues it. These are the tools that hold a fixed or managed system at its target.

cards.front: Define competitive devaluation — and its risks.
cards.back:
Competitive devaluation: when a government deliberately pushes down the value of its currency to make exports cheaper and gain a trade advantage.

The risks:

  • Retaliation — rivals devalue too, a "currency war" that shrinks global trade.
  • Imported inflation — dearer imports cut consumers' purchasing power.
  • A heavier foreign-denominated debt burden, threatening financial instability.

cards.front: Evaluate the impact of a depreciation across the macro objectives.
cards.back:
Cheaper exports and dearer imports tend to improve the current account, boost growth and cut unemployment in export industries — the mirror image of an appreciation.

The costs:

  • Imported inflation plus demand-pull pressure from rising export demand.
  • Lower living standards as import prices erode purchasing power.

Which effect dominates depends on the economy's trade exposure and the elasticities of export and import demand.

cards.front: Show the J-curve — and state the Marshall-Lerner condition.
cards.back:
After a depreciation the current account worsens first: contracts fix prices in the short run and consumers are slow to switch, so PEDx and PEDm are inelastic.

Only as they adjust does the balance improve through the long run — tracing a J.

The Marshall-Lerner condition: a depreciation improves the current account only if PEDx + PEDm > 1. If combined demand is inelastic, it worsens instead.
cards.svgAlt: J-curve diagram of the net trade balance against time: after a depreciation the deficit deepens in the short run, bottoms out, then improves into surplus in the long run

cards.front: Define international competitiveness — and how is it measured?
cards.back:
International competitiveness: the ability of a country's goods and services to compete successfully in global markets.

Two key measures, both relative to rivals:

  • Relative unit labour costs — rising faster than competitors' signals weakening competitiveness.
  • Relative export prices, where higher prices than competitors' usually mean the same.

cards.front: State the unit labour costs formula — and how is it read?
cards.back:
Unit labour costs = total labour costs ÷ total output.

It measures the labour cost of each unit produced, so it captures wages and productivity together: wages can rise without harming competitiveness if output per worker rises as fast. What matters is unit labour costs relative to competitors.
cards.formulaHtml: Unitlabourcosts=totallabourcosts÷totaloutputUnit labour costs = total labour costs ÷ total outputUnitlabourcosts=totallabourcosts÷totaloutput

cards.front: Country A spends £5.4m on labour to produce 900 units; Country B spends £6.5m to produce 1,000 units. Compare their unit labour costs.
cards.back:
• A: 5,400,000 ÷ 900 = £6,000 per unit.
  • B: 6,500,000 ÷ 1,000 = £6,500 per unit.

B's total wage bill is larger, but so is its output — yet B's unit labour cost is still about 8% higher, so on this measure A is the more cost-competitive.

Total labour spending alone says nothing: only cost per unit does.

cards.front: What factors influence international competitiveness?
cards.back:
Cost factors

  • Relative unit labour costs.
  • The exchange rate (a weaker currency cheapens exports).
  • Relative inflation.
  • Productivity, which lowers cost per unit.

Non-cost factors

  • Innovation and technology.
  • Quality and branding that command premium prices.
  • Infrastructure and logistics — transport, energy and digital networks that keep firms efficient.

cards.front: Why does international competitiveness matter — and what happens when it is lost?
cards.back:
Competitive: exports grow, improving the current account; growth and investment strengthen; export industries expand employment.

Uncompetitive: the same channels run in reverse — falling exports worsen the current account, growth and investment slow, and export industries shed jobs, risking a persistent deficit. Because competitiveness is relative, standing still while rivals improve is itself a decline.

cards.front: Distinguish absolute poverty from relative poverty.
cards.back:
Absolute poverty: individuals cannot afford the basic necessities for survival, such as food, water, shelter, and healthcare — measured against a fixed international threshold, e.g. the World Bank's poverty line of $2.15 per day (2022 PPP).

Relative poverty: household income falls below a set proportion of median income in an economy — in the UK, below 60% of median household income.

cards.front: What changes absolute poverty?
cards.back:
• Economic growth in developing countries raises incomes and employment, pulling people over the fixed threshold.
  • Government policies — welfare benefits, subsidies and public services — support the poorest directly.
  • Global factors — trade, foreign aid and investment — shape poverty in developing countries.
  • Natural disasters and conflicts push it the other way by destroying livelihoods and infrastructure.

cards.front: What changes relative poverty?
cards.back:
Because relative poverty is measured against median income, it moves with the income distribution:

  • The skills gap in education drives wage disparities.
  • Demographic changes — ageing populations, shifting household composition — alter who falls below the line.
  • Government tax and welfare policy redistributes income directly.
  • Labour market changes — unemployment, underemployment and low wages — push relative poverty up.

cards.front: Distinguish income inequality from wealth inequality.
cards.back:
Income inequality: the unequal distribution of earnings, such as wages, rent, interest, and profit. Income is a flow of money over a period of time.

Wealth inequality: the unequal distribution of assets, such as property, shares, and savings. Wealth is a stock of monetary value at a point in time.

cards.front: Show how the Lorenz curve illustrates inequality.
cards.back:
The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative percentage of total income or wealth against the cumulative percentage of the population. The 45° diagonal is the line of perfect equality — everyone has the same; the Lorenz curve shows the actual distribution.

The further the curve bows from the diagonal, the greater the inequality. Area A (between the two) against area A + B (everything under the diagonal) gives the Gini coefficient.
cards.svgAlt: Lorenz curve diagram with a 45 degree line of perfect equality, the Lorenz curve bowing below it, area A between the two lines and area B beneath the Lorenz curve

cards.front: How is the Gini coefficient calculated from the Lorenz curve — and how is it read?
cards.back:
Gini coefficient = A ÷ (A + B): the area between the line of perfect equality and the Lorenz curve (A), as a ratio of the total area under the line of perfect equality (A + B).

0 means perfect equality, 1 means perfect inequality — so a higher Gini coefficient means greater inequality.
cards.formulaHtml: Ginicoefficient=A÷(A+B)Gini coefficient = A ÷ (A + B)Ginicoefficient=A÷(A+B)

cards.front: What causes income and wealth inequality?
cards.back:
• Education and skills — unequal access drives wage disparities.
  • The tax system — progressive taxation redistributes towards lower incomes.
  • Welfare payments — support the disposable income of the poorest.
  • The minimum wage — lifts the lowest earners.
  • Trade unions — negotiate better pay for low- and middle-income workers.
  • The distribution of assets itself: who already holds property and financial investments shapes the income they generate.

cards.front: What does the Kuznets curve hypothesise about development and inequality?
cards.back:
As an economy develops, inequality first rises and then falls after a turning point — an inverted U against real GDP per capita.

Early on, urbanisation and industrialisation raise inequality: those in the industrial sector out-earn those left in agriculture. As development continues, education, social mobility and government intervention — progressive taxation and welfare — pull inequality back down.
cards.svgAlt: Kuznets curve diagram: an inverted U of income inequality against economic development, peaking at the dashed boundary between developing and developed economies

cards.front: What is the significance of capitalism for inequality?
cards.back:
Capitalism: an economic system based on private ownership of the factors of production with the aim of generating profit.

It rewards individuals by their ability to generate profit, so disparities in income and wealth follow — and they compound: those who own capital accumulate wealth more easily than those who rely solely on wages. Some inequality is thus built into capitalism's incentive structure.

cards.front: Evaluate: does inequality help or harm an economy?
cards.back:
Benefits: some inequality creates incentives to work, innovate and take risks; encourages investment in human capital; and rewards contribution, aiding efficient resource allocation.

Costs: extreme inequality demotivates those who see the system as unfair; entrenches social immobility where the disadvantaged cannot access education and opportunity; and widens health and living-standard disparities. The question is not whether to have inequality but how much.

cards.front: Distinguish economic growth from economic development.
cards.back:
Economic growth is the narrower concept, measured by increases in real GDP.

Economic development: a broader concept. It includes economic growth but also considers improvements in living standards, welfare, and quality of life — non-material factors such as health, education and equality. Growth does not automatically mean development.

cards.front: Distinguish single from composite indicators of development.
cards.back:
Single indicators measure one aspect of development — the infant mortality rate, literacy rate, or access to clean water. Useful for specific comparisons, but each gives only a partial picture.

Composite indicators combine several single indicators into one index for a more rounded view — the HDI is the leading example.

cards.front: What are the three dimensions of the HDI — and how is it scored?
cards.back:
The UN's Human Development Index combines three equally weighted elements:

  • Health (life expectancy at birth).
  • Education (mean years of schooling for adults, expected years for children).
  • Income (real GNI per capita at PPP, adjusting for cost-of-living differences).

Countries score between 0 and 1 — Norway 0.961, Niger 0.394 — with higher scores meaning higher human development.

cards.front: Evaluate the HDI as a measure of development.
cards.back:
For: a composite measure capturing more than income; enables international comparisons; puts health and education alongside GDP.

Against: it hides inequality within countries — two countries with the same HDI can distribute opportunity very differently; ignores sustainability and the environment; and rests on data quality that is often unreliable in developing countries — life expectancy figures are estimates.

cards.front: Name other indicators of development beyond the HDI.
cards.back:
• The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) across health, education and living standards.
  • The Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI), discounting the HDI for inequality.
  • GNI per capita.
  • Access to clean water and sanitation.
  • Environmental indicators (emissions, deforestation, biodiversity loss — is development sustainable?).
  • The Human Poverty Index and the Social Progress Index.

cards.front: How does primary product dependency hold back development?
cards.back:
An economy reliant on exporting raw materials or agricultural products faces price volatility — commodity prices swing, so export revenues are unstable — and a limited ability to add value, capping long-run growth in real GDP.

It also risks Dutch disease: a primary-product boom drives the currency up, pricing the country's other exports out of world markets.

cards.front: What is the savings gap — and what does the Harrod-Domar model say about it?
cards.back:
The savings gap: the difference between the savings available for investment in an economy and the amount needed to achieve the desired rate of growth.

The Harrod-Domar model suggests that economic growth is directly related to the level of savings and investment in an economy: a higher savings rate funds more investment in capital goods, raising productivity and growth — so a savings gap traps poor countries in low growth.

cards.front: Define the foreign currency gap and capital flight.
cards.back:
Foreign currency gap: occurs when a country does not have enough foreign currency to pay for essential imports — machinery, technology, raw materials — often because reserves are drained by debt payments or a persistent trade deficit.

Capital flight: the rapid outflow of financial assets and capital driven by economic or political instability, stripping the economy of funds for domestic investment.

cards.front: What other economic factors influence growth and development?
cards.back:
• Demographics — rapid population growth strains resources, ageing shrinks the workforce.
  • Debt — servicing it diverts resources from investment and scares off FDI.
  • Access to credit and banking — without it, individuals and firms cannot fund productive investment.
  • Infrastructure — poor transport, communication and energy raise costs and cut off markets.
  • Education and skills build the human capital growth needs.
  • An absence of property rights undermines it all: without secure legal ownership, why invest or innovate?

cards.front: What non-economic factors influence growth and development?
cards.back:
• Corruption — diverts resources from productive investment, distorts decisions and raises costs.
  • Poor governance and political instability — create uncertainty, deter foreign investment and waste resources.
  • Conflict and war — destroy physical capital and can set development back decades.
  • Geography — being landlocked or facing difficult terrain raises transport costs and weakens trade competitiveness.

cards.front: Name the six market-orientated development strategies.
cards.back:
Trade liberalisation (cut tariffs, grow through trade), promotion of FDI (foreign capital, technology and expertise), removal of government subsidies (efficiency and freed spending), floating exchange rates (self-correcting trade imbalances), microfinance (small loans for those outside banking), and privatisation (profit incentives for efficiency).

All rely on free market forces and the private sector to drive development.

cards.front: Name the six interventionist development strategies.
cards.back:
• Development of human capital (education and healthcare).
  • Protectionism (shelter domestic industries while they grow).
  • Managed exchange rates (stability for exporters and investors).
  • Infrastructure development (transport, energy, communications).
  • Joint ventures with global companies (investment and technology transfer).
  • Buffer stock schemes (stabilise commodity prices).

All are government-led actions designed to correct market failure and direct development.

cards.front: Show how a buffer stock scheme stabilises a commodity price.
cards.back:
The scheme defends a band between Pmax and Pmin. In a normal year S1 sets P1 inside the band. A good harvest (S2) would push the price to P2, below the floor — so the scheme buys stock, moving supply back towards S1. A bad harvest (S3) would send the price to P3, above the ceiling — so it sells stock.

Stable prices smooth producers' incomes, encouraging investment in the sector — if the scheme can afford to hold the stock and judges the band well.
cards.svgAlt: Commodity market diagram with demand, three supply curves and a price band: a good harvest pushes the price below the floor so the scheme buys stock, a bad harvest pushes it above the ceiling so the scheme sells, keeping the price between Pmax and Pmin

cards.front: What does the Lewis model say about industrialisation — and what are its limits?
cards.back:
The Lewis model: explains how labour from the agricultural sector can be transferred to the industrial sector, leading to economic growth and development — industry adds more value, raising real national income and living standards.

Its limits:

  • It assumes surplus agricultural labour, which may not exist.
  • It ignores industrialisation's negative externalities — environmental degradation and social inequality.

Related routes: tourism (foreign exchange, but fragile) and primary industries (comparative advantage, but volatile).

cards.front: Evaluate Fairtrade, foreign aid and debt relief as development strategies.
cards.back:
• Fairtrade guarantees minimum prices and premiums, raising producer incomes — but reaches few producers, and higher consumer prices limit demand.
  • Aid (grants, soft loans, humanitarian support) funds vital projects — but can create dependency, be misallocated, or serve donors' political agendas.
  • Debt relief frees resources for development and improves creditworthiness — but leaves structural problems untouched, and without fiscal discipline new debt simply accumulates.

cards.front: Contrast the roles of the World Bank, the IMF and NGOs in development.
cards.back:
• The World Bank aims to reduce poverty through long-term loans for infrastructure and development projects, plus technical assistance.
  • The IMF promotes global financial stability with short-term loans for balance-of-payments crises — usually with conditions, such as structural adjustment programmes and austerity.
  • NGOs — non-profits independent of governments, like Oxfam — deliver aid, run development projects and advocate on specific issues such as education, healthcare and human rights.

cards.front: What are the five functions of financial markets?
cards.back:
• Facilitate saving — deposits, bonds and equities let households and firms earn a return and accumulate wealth (and, per Harrod-Domar, savings fund growth).
  • Lend to businesses and individuals for investment and consumption.
  • Facilitate the exchange of goods and services through money and payment systems.
  • Provide forward markets in currencies and commodities, letting firms hedge price risk.
  • Provide a market for equities, so firms can raise capital by issuing shares.

cards.front: How do asymmetric information and externalities cause financial market failure?
cards.back:
Asymmetric information — one party knows more than the other: lenders cannot tell high-risk from low-risk borrowers (adverse selection, raising rates and choking lending), and consumers misjudge products they do not understand, from payday loans to complex investments.

Negative externalities — excessive risk-taking by banks imposes costs on third parties: the 2008 collapse of Lehman Brothers triggered a global recession and widespread job losses.

cards.front: Define moral hazard, speculation and market rigging in the financial sector.
cards.back:
Moral hazard: occurs when individuals or institutions take on excessive risk because they do not bear the full consequences of their actions — banks expecting bailouts, or the insured taking chances they otherwise would not.

Speculation: buying assets purely expecting prices to rise, inflating bubbles that burst into instability.

Market rigging: manipulating markets for private gain — the LIBOR scandal — distorting prices and destroying trust.

cards.front: What are the consequences of financial market failure for the wider economy?
cards.back:
• Systemic risk — trouble in one institution spreads through the whole system into financial crisis.
  • Loss of confidence — collapsing trust brings bank runs and panic.
  • Real economic damage — recession, unemployment and lost output follow financial failure.
  • Inequity — taxpayers end up bearing the cost of bailing out private institutions.

cards.front: What are the key functions of a central bank?
cards.back:
• Implementing monetary policy — the Bank of England's MPC sets interest rates (and QE at the zero lower bound) to meet the government's 2% CPI inflation target.
  • Banker to the government — managing its accounts and issuing its debt.
  • Banker to the banks — central banks act as a lender of last resort to commercial banks and other financial institutions in times of financial stress, providing emergency funding in a liquidity crisis.
  • Regulating the banking system.

cards.front: How does the Bank of England regulate the banking system?
cards.back:
Through two arms. The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) sets rules for individual banks — minimum capital and liquidity requirements, tested against shocks by stress tests.

The Financial Policy Committee (FPC) watches the system as a whole, deploying macroprudential tools — such as loan-to-value limits — against excessive credit growth and asset bubbles that could threaten financial stability.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: Distinguish the three types of public expenditure.
cards.back:
Current expenditure: day-to-day spending on public sector wages, such as payments to teachers and nurses, and on the consumption of goods and services such as medicines and utilities.

Capital expenditure: long-term investment in infrastructure — roads, hospitals, schools — raising productive potential.

Transfer payments: payments with no good or service received in return — pensions, benefits, subsidies — which redistribute income but do not directly add to GDP.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: Why do the size and composition of public expenditure change over time?
cards.back:
• Economic growth lifts tax revenue and cuts transfer payments, freeing spending for services.
  • Demographic change — an ageing population — raises pension and healthcare spending.
  • Political priorities shift money between sectors.
  • External shocks — recessions, pandemics — force up transfers and stimulus.
  • Technological change alters what public services cost and need, such as digital infrastructure.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: Evaluate the significance of public expenditure as a share of GDP.
cards.back:
For a bigger state: infrastructure, education and health spending raise productivity and LRAS; services and transfers lift living standards and equality.

Against:

  • Crowding out — government borrowing bids up interest rates, squeezing private investment and consumption.
  • Higher spending eventually means higher taxes, cutting disposable income.

The verdict turns on what the money buys: capital spending that grows the economy, or current spending that must be financed forever.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: Distinguish progressive, proportional and regressive taxes — and how do direct and indirect taxes map onto them?
cards.back:
• Progressive: a tax where the percentage of income paid in tax rises as income rises — income tax, inheritance tax.
  • Proportional: the percentage stays constant at every income.
  • Regressive: the percentage falls as income rises — VAT and duties on tobacco and alcohol.

Direct taxes (on income or profits: income tax, corporation tax, National Insurance) tend to be progressive; indirect taxes (on spending: VAT, excise duties) tend to be regressive.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: Show the Laffer curve — and why can a higher tax rate raise less revenue?
cards.back:
Revenue is zero at a 0% tax rate and at 100%: in between, revenue rises to a peak and then falls. Raising the rate from t1 to t2 cuts revenue from R1 to R2.

Beyond the peak, higher rates blunt incentives to work and invest, drive avoidance and evasion, and push skilled workers and capital abroad — brain drain and capital flight — shrinking the tax base faster than the rate rises.
cards.svgAlt: Laffer curve: total tax revenue rises with the tax rate to a peak and then falls, with the rise from t1 to t2 cutting revenue from R1 to R2

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: Evaluate the economic effects of raising taxes.
cards.back:
Higher income tax weakens incentives to work, shrinking labour supply; but progressive taxes narrow income inequality, while regressive ones widen it. Lower disposable income cuts consumption, so real output and employment fall; higher indirect taxes raise costs and feed cost-push inflation.

The trade balance can go either way — less consumption means fewer imports, but weaker domestic production invites them back. And higher corporation tax deters FDI, while cuts attract it.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: Distinguish automatic stabilisers from discretionary fiscal policy.
cards.back:
Automatic stabilisers: non-discretionary changes in government spending and taxation that occur automatically in response to changes in economic activity, helping to stabilise the economic cycle without the government intervening. In a boom, tax revenue rises and welfare spending falls; in a recession, the reverse — the deficit widens and cushions demand by itself.

Discretionary fiscal policy: deliberate changes in spending and taxation to influence economic activity.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: Distinguish a fiscal deficit from the national debt — and cyclical from structural deficits.
cards.back:
A fiscal deficit: government spending exceeds taxation revenue in a given period — it resets each year.

The national debt: the total amount of money that a government owes to creditors — the accumulation of past deficits and surpluses over time.

A cyclical deficit follows the economic cycle, widening in recession and narrowing in boom.

A structural deficit persists even at potential output — a fundamental imbalance the cycle will not fix.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: What influences the size of fiscal deficits and the national debt?
cards.back:
• Economic growth — strong growth lifts tax revenue and trims welfare spending.
  • Interest rates — higher rates raise the cost of servicing existing debt.
  • Government spending priorities and taxation policy set the balance directly.

Then the pressures:

  • Demographic change (ageing populations demand more welfare and healthcare).
  • External shocks — crises, pandemics, disasters — that force spending up as revenue falls.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: Why do large deficits and high national debt matter?
cards.back:
• Economic stability — eroding confidence raises borrowing costs and deters investment; persistent deficits risk credit-rating downgrades and, at the limit, a debt crisis.
  • Intergenerational equity — future taxpayers inherit the repayments.
  • Inflation — financing deficits by printing money debases the currency.
  • Policy flexibility — a heavily indebted government has little fiscal room left when the next shock arrives.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: What policies address fiscal deficits and debt, and poverty and inequality, in a global context?
cards.back:
Deficits and debt

  • Fiscal austerity (spending cuts, tax rises) to restore confidence.
  • Structural reforms — labour markets, pensions, public-service efficiency — to grow revenue.
  • Debt restructuring with creditors: longer repayment, lower rates, or partial write-off.

Poverty and inequality: progressive taxation, social welfare programmes, and investment in education and healthcare to raise social mobility.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: How can governments control global companies — and what limits them?
cards.back:
Tools:

  • Regulation (antitrust, environmental and labour standards).
  • Taxation — including rules against transfer pricing, where an MNC prices sales between its own subsidiaries to shift profits into low-tax jurisdictions.
  • International cooperation through the OECD and UN.

The limits:

  • Global firms can relocate to friendlier regimes.
  • They can exploit regulatory arbitrage between countries.
  • Effective control ultimately requires international coordination no single government can impose.

cards.topic: 4.5 Role of the state in the macroeconomy
cards.front: Evaluate the problems facing policymakers in a global economy.
cards.back:
• Inaccurate information — policy is set on data and forecasts that are often wrong or incomplete, producing unintended consequences.
  • Risks and uncertainties — economic shocks, geopolitical events and shifting global markets defy prediction.
  • An inability to control external shocks — global crises arrive regardless of domestic policy; governments can only respond, with monetary, fiscal and exchange-rate tools whose effects come with lags.

Policy in an interconnected world is damage limitation as much as control.
